subject: seahorse
pitch: A lined seahorse holding on to a strand of seagrass with its curled tail. A ridged body in sunny yellow with thin dark lines and a few white freckles, a little crown of spikes on its head, a long tube snout, a delicate fluttering fin on its back, and big, curious eyes.
reasoning:
I should stick to conservative, well-documented API calls like createBuilder, b.joint, b.chain, b.sweep, and b.part rather than riskier ones. I'm thinking through proportions for the seahorse model, roughly 15-20cm tall like a real lined seahorse, with the seagrass strand taller at around 0.35m.

Now I'm planning the skeleton: a root "hips" joint, then a spine chain running from tail curl to head, built with manually-placed joints or b.chain given a path and options for joint count and role. I'm weighing whether b.sweep accepts a radius function that varies along the path versus just a flat number, since using a function risks failing if the API only expects a scalar.

I'm reconsidering a safer approach -- building the body from parts (spheres/capsules) attached to explicit joint bones rather than relying on chain's unclear joint return, and checking whether part() supports scale and whether rod-like geometry between two points needs a custom part with aim/dir orientation.

Instead of trusting scale shortcuts, I'll write a helper function that generates a scaled sphere geometry for ellipsoid-shaped body segments, then start planning the seahorse's spine as a series of points -- head tilted forward, belly bulging toward +Z, back along -Z, tail curling forward beneath.

Working out the tail curl now: it needs to wrap around a grass stem, so I'm placing the stem at a fixed position and defining the tail as a circular arc around it, tracing down the back, along the bottom, then gripping upward at the front.

Continuing the spiral coil math for the tail tip, I'm checking that it doesn't overlap the body geometry before moving on to defining the trunk joints—hips, spine segments, neck, and head positions.

Now I'm roughing out the body blobs: belly, chest, and neck ellipsoids with their center positions and radii, then placing the head sphere and starting the snout cylinder extending forward from the face.

Working out a function to place belly rings around the ellipsoid body, scaling thin torus tubes to match the cross-section width at each height level so they hug the body's curvature naturally.

I'm also adding dorsal ridge spikes along the back using small cones, and scattering tiny flattened white sphere freckles across the body sides by computing their positions along the ellipsoid surface using azimuth angles.

Now I'm building the eyes with a gold ring sphere, dark pupil, and white highlight placed on each side of the head, plus a coronet of small arced cones forming a crown spike pattern at the top of the head.

For the dorsal fin, I'm considering options like thin flat box rays or an extrude-based fan shape along the back, weighing uncertainty in the extrude function's color argument against building the fin from simpler parts directly.

Still positioning fin rays and colors...

Now thinking through the tail construction: since seahorse tails are square in cross-section, I'm using box geometries for the segments instead of cylinders, oriented along each joint direction with proper up-vector alignment to keep the square faces twisted correctly along the curl.

I'm adding thin dark bands at each joint for the segmented ring look, tapering the tail radius from thick near the body to thin at the tip. For the seagrass, I'm building wavy blades from stacked thin boxes following a sine-curved path so they pass naturally near the tail's coiled center.

Now I'm working out extra blades positioned behind the main one at slight x-offsets and shorter heights, tilting them outward while checking they don't collide with the tail's thicker radius at low y-values.

I'll keep the grass static and attach it to its own joint under root, while the seahorse hangs from a "hips" joint parented to root. Now I'm setting up the skeleton structure, starting with the root and hips joints at their model-space positions.

Still defining joints...

Working through the spine, neck, head, and jaw joint positions, each parented to the previous one, then moving to the tail chain which branches off hips with its segments following an arc computed from angular positions around a curve.

Continuing the tail curl, I'm tapering the radius at each joint down toward the tip and adding small ridge nubs angled outward along the curve, plus a tip sphere. Then I'm shifting to the body blobs, assigning belly to hips, chest to spine2, neck and head to their bones, and starting on the belly ring details.

Writing ring generation code...

Since the faceted low-poly sphere hides rings at exactly 1.0 scale, I'll nudge the ring placement factor up to 1.04 so it pokes outside the surface properly. I also want to add small ridge bumps as cones along the back and chest ring heights, angled outward and colored to match the ridge detailing.

Now I'm working out freckle placement, scattering small flattened white spheres across the sides using randomized angles and offsets so they sit partially embedded in the surface. Then I'm setting up the head as an ellipsoid with specific proportions, adding brow bumps, and building the snout base as a cylinder extending from the forehead area.

Now I'm defining the snout cylinder's direction vector and tapered radii, plus a smaller wedge-shaped cylinder underneath for the lower jaw, positioning it at the jaw joint offset along the snout direction and slightly downward.

Adding dark mouth tip and ring bands along the snout, computing the normalized snout direction vector for placement, then positioning the eyes symmetrically on either side of the head blob.

Now I'm placing the eyeballs with gold-ish spheres, dark pupils, and tiny white highlight dots, checking they sit just at the head's surface. Then I'm laying out five crown spikes arrayed across the top of the head, computing their base positions and directions outward and upward with tapering lengths and radii.

Next I'm adding a row of back-of-neck ridge cones running down the spine, placing pectoral fin plates near the shoulders with pale coloring and fine rays, and setting up the dorsal fin joint attached to the spine for its fin geometry.

Working out fin ray placements...

Now moving to grass blades: I'm defining a blade-generation function that samples points along a curve with lean and sway controlled by a sine phase, building out each blade's shape and color per joint.

Still writing blade geometry...

Now I'm placing the remaining three blades around the main one, adjusting their x/z offsets, lean angles, and heights to fan them out behind the seahorse's body near the tail.

Then I'm adding a sand mound ellipsoid beneath the seahorse with a few scattered pebbles, and making sure the lowest points of the mound and tail keep the figure stably grounded before writing out the final part export code.
